name: Brachypodium distachyon NaN0598B Resequencing

alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

name: Aspergillus nidulans FP-2403-3 Gene Expression profiling - AN60

alt_names.name: Validation of the transfer of sugar catabolism model from Aspergillus niger to other fungi using an orthology-based approach

description: Using the high quality manually curated genome sequence of Aspergillus niger NRRL3 and a large transcriptomic dataset on individual monomeric sugars, the authors have constructed a model for sugar catabolism. This model has the potential of being a reference for other fungi, but to which extent the knowledge can easily be transferred is not known. In this study, the authors aim to test the potential and limits of transferring this model to other fungi using an orthology-based approach combined with omics-analysis on relevant carbon sources to compare the response in different fungi.

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description:
Peatland ecosystems represent 3-5% of the land surface, but sequester 12-30% of soil organic carbon. However, this very large pool of carbon is vulnerable to oxidation as a function of climate change. Increased temperatures and lowered water tables with climate change or anthropogenic drainage can shift peatlands from being net carbon sinks to net carbon sources, but the rate of carbon loss from peatlands subjected to climate change treatments varies widely. The net effects of increased temperature and decreased water availability in peatlands could drive significant changes in peatland carbon balance and methane efflux directly by accelerating peat oxidation or net primary production, and indirectly by altering plant community composition.  
 
Microbial communities involved in C cycling in peatlands have been characterized piecemeal via a variety of approaches, making a comprehensive understanding of community organization and comparison of communities among peatlands impossible. In particular, the relative importance of fungi, bacteria and archaea in peatlands, and the relative importance of free-living heterotrophs vs. mycorrhizal fungi, are poorly understood, but are likely to vary depending on a variety of factors, including dominance of mycorrhizal and non-mycorrhizal hosts, pH, redox potential, carbon quality, phenolic concentrations and nutrient availability. These communities of fungi and bacteria are likely to differ in their expression of extracellular enzymes for mobilization of C. In particular, ericoid mycorrhizal fungi (ErMF), because they receive a labile carbon subsidy from their host plants, may inhibit lignolytic fungi and bacteria in their mycorrhizospheres. However, these ErMF themselves have a broad range of enzyme activity in vitro, producing extracellular enzymes capable of cellulytic and partial lignolytic activity. The in vivo potential and complete suite of extracellular enzymes produced by these fungi is poorly known. Discovery of the potential suite of extracellular enzymes for these organisms will provide the basis for understanding community potential for regulating C cycling. Metatranscriptome analyses will provide us with a foundation for characterizing the functional potential of different microbial communities as they interact with the contrasting environments created by roots of different plant functional groups in interaction with changing temperature and water table. This will serve as the jumping off point for enhanced models of peatland C cycling that incorporate microbial community structure and function. The large scale microbial profiling will be linked to measures of C cycling (CO2 and CH4 flux at a minimum, plus ecosystem C balance, enzyme assays, DOC quantity and quality at some sites) and environmental conditions (pH, Eh, water table height, plant communities, temperature) in order to understand the factors that structure these communities, and test hypotheses and develop models for microbial community regulation of peatland C cycling.  
 
The diverse redox conditions experienced by the organisms in these systems generate complex microbial consortia involved in use of a wide array of substrates and electron acceptors. As redox and substrate quality decline with depth generally gradients from aerobic heterotrophs and plant associated organisms at the surface, to organisms using lower energy substrates through fermentative pathways, and methanogens prevail at depth. The organisms along such gradients represent key but poorly understood players in the global balance of C and balance of trace gas fluxes (e.g. CO2 vs CH4) that prevail under changing conditions. Using single cell sequencing techniques we can target taxa active over these steep gradients to improve our understanding of the microbial players and processes that regulate trace gas flux. Of particular interest are those microbes specifically associated with the steep redox gradients associated with plant roots.

alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

alt_names.name: Validation of the transfer of sugar catabolism model from Aspergillus niger to other fungi using an orthology-based approach

description: Using the high quality manually curated genome sequence of Aspergillus niger NRRL3 and a large transcriptomic dataset on individual monomeric sugars, the authors have constructed a model for sugar catabolism. This model has the potential of being a reference for other fungi, but to which extent the knowledge can easily be transferred is not known. In this study, the authors aim to test the potential and limits of transferring this model to other fungi using an orthology-based approach combined with omics-analysis on relevant carbon sources to compare the response in different fungi.

name: unclassified "LHC4-1" archaeon JGI MDM2 LHC4sed-1-I9

alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description: Using the high quality manually curated genome sequence of Aspergillus niger NRRL3 and a large transcriptomic dataset on individual monomeric sugars, the authors have constructed a model for sugar catabolism. alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

name: Fervidibacteria bacterium JGI MDM2 LHC4sed-1-G17

alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

name: Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3 Transposon library T8repB_Jun

alt_names.name: Marine bacterioplanktonic communities from the University of Georgia, USA  for heterotrophic carbon processing in the sea

description:
Heterotrophic marine bacterioplankton are the principal consumers of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in the oceans. As the largest living surface area in the sea, they detect, transport, and assimilate bioreactive constituents from the DOM pool, transforming these compounds to particulate matter or recycling them back to their inorganic forms. Despite the importance of this activity on a global scale, progress in understanding bacterioplankton-mediated DOM flux has been slow. Functional genomic/metagenomic approaches have the potential to uncover major insights into DOM fate, but are limited by the mismatch between the pace of finding new genes and the pace of determining their function. 
 
We would leverage an existing model organism system based on the marine Roseobacter Ruegeria (formerly Silicibacter) pomeroyi DSS-3 to improve understanding of the genetic basis of bacterial DOM cycling in the ocean. A whole genome negative selection framework will be applied to R. pomeroyi DSS-3 to identify genes required for transformation of selected compounds or compound classes representative of the DOM pool. Since this is a 'negative selection' approach, it is restricted to DOM compounds that can support growth of the model bacterium (making the large genome and substrate promiscuity of R. pomeroyi advantageous) and compounds that are degraded by only one pathway in the bacterium. 
 
Transposon mutant libraries of R. pomeroyi DSS-3 will be challenged in batch culture for the ability to grow on organic compounds representative of the marine DOM pool (for example, selected sugars, organic acids, aromatic compounds, and amino acids). The surviving mutant pool for each compound will be screened with Illumina sequencing, using deep sequencing of the transposon-gene junctions. When mapped to the R. pomeroyi DSS-3 genome, coverage gaps will indicate the location of essential genes, since mutants with a transposon insertion in an essential gene will be unable to grow. Enrichment of the transposon-gene junctions prior to sequencing will be carried out by affinity purification. This whole-genome negative selection approach has been given the acronym 'HITS' for 'high-throughput insertion tracking by deep sequencing'. Mutants absent in all surviving mutant pools will allow ust to distinguish core genes (which are not of interest here) from genes necessary for the selected DOM transformations. 
 
Genes identified by HITS in the R. pomeroyi model system will be evaluated for their ecological relevance. For a selected subset of compounds, quantitative metatranscriptomic analyses will be carried out using natural marine bacterial communities and experimental manipulation of the concentration of the compounds. Transcriptional response of the natural marine community for the candidate genes and associated pathways will be characterized.

name: Brachypodium distachyon Bd21-3 NaN0779 Resequencing

alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

name: Populus trichocarpa 368 Gene Expression Profiling - 368_N_1_18_24

alt_names.name: RNA-seq analysis of Populus trichocarpa genotypes

description: RNA-seq on Populus trichocarpa genotypes. These genotypes tend to have high total sugar content as well as above average growth characteristics. RNA-seq will provide a whole genome look at transcripts being affected by gene mutations in a natural populus population. This information will be used to do network analysis with the idea that it will aid in understanding the molecular basis for observed phenotypes and how to overcome recalcitrance in Populus biomass.

name: Trichoderma reesei QM6a Gene Expression Profiling - TrCS4.2

alt_names.name: Validation of the transfer of sugar catabolism model from Aspergillus niger to other fungi using an orthology-based approach

description: Using the high quality manually curated genome sequence of Aspergillus niger NRRL3 and a large transcriptomic dataset on individual monomeric sugars, the authors have constructed a model for sugar catabolism. This model has the potential of being a reference for other fungi, but to which extent the knowledge can easily be transferred is not known. In this study, the authors aim to test the potential and limits of transferring this model to other fungi using an orthology-based approach combined with omics-analysis on relevant carbon sources to compare the response in different fungi.

name: Aigarchaeota archaeon JGI MDM2 JNZ-1-G18

alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

alt_names.name: Soil microbial communities from Nicasio Native Grass Ranch, CA for soil carbon cycle studies

description: We propose an integrative effort to link geochemical data with novel genomics approaches to identify and functionally characterize microbial communities involved in soil C storage, in particular under improved land management techniques of composting and vertical subsoiling. Rangeland sites in California, at the Nicasio Native Grass Ranch provide access to long-term experimental plots undergoing two different land management practices; (1) soil compost amendment and (2) Yeoman subsoiling plow. These plots will serve as sampling sites for the proposed study (Fig. 1). These practices have been found to increase (compost) and decrease (subsoiler) soil C storage and thus provide an excellent template upon which to explore the role of microbial community composition and activity on soil C dynamics. We will sample soils along three replicated transects at three depths (0-10cm, 10-20cm, 20-30cm) in each plot (n = 9 treatment and 3 control plots) on a monthly basis for 24 months. Additional experiments will establish new composting and subsoiling treatments in similarly replicated plots. Beyond the biological sampling we will measure soil respiration rates, soil chemical and physical properties, microclimate characteristics, hydrolytic and oxidative enzyme activities, and collect soil C quantity and quality measurements. These provide important correlates for C fluxes; C quality measurements and enzyme assays will allow to better link composition to function across scales. Biological samples will be analyzed as a whole, in addition to being used for spatial, random and functional community sub-sampling. The DNA and RNA from the total community will be used for shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and SSU rRNA iTag sequencing. Functionally and spatially enriched sub-communities as well as meso-genomes will be targeted for shotgun metagenomics and SSU rRNA iTags. Specifically, we will be comparing the overall community structure (functional and phylogenetic) to the active community and assess differences (and/or shifts) over time, with soil depth, and with differing soil treatment, and moreover how these relate to soil C storage. This will allow us to pinpoint potential key players in the C sequestration process and decipher their functional capabilities to model their impact on soil C storage. The reduced complexity of the active microbial communities will allow us to link phylogeny and function most efficiently. Metagenome assembly will be more tractable and enabled by the meso-genomes, and metatrancriptome data will be mappable on active sub-community metagenomes, bringing soil genomics to a new level.

alt_names.name: Validation of the transfer of sugar catabolism model from Aspergillus niger to other fungi using an orthology-based approach

description: Using the high quality manually curated genome sequence of Aspergillus niger NRRL3 and a large transcriptomic dataset on individual monomeric sugars, the authors have constructed a model for sugar catabolism. This model has the potential of being a reference for other fungi, but to which extent the knowledge can easily be transferred is not known. In this study, the authors aim to test the potential and limits of transferring this model to other fungi using an orthology-based approach combined with omics-analysis on relevant carbon sources to compare the response in different fungi.

name: Fervidibacter sacchari PD1

alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

name: Brachypodium distachyon NaN1039 Resequencing

alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. description: The methanome comprises genomic information distributed across organisms that either produce or consume methane as part of their metabolic repertoire. The methanome thus encodes information that regulates methane cycling in natural and engineered ecosystems both impacting climate and the efficacy of industrial process. We have chosen a suite of sample sites that together capture key underexplored niches in the methanosphere. Data arising from this study will provide an information reservoir for researchers and educators interested in exploring diversity and metabolic complexity of natural and engineered microbial communities. Information on ecology and niche adaptation of methanogens and methanotrophs will provide key information critical to incorporating microbial traits into predictive models of global methane budgets.

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

The methanome thus encodes information that regulates methane cycling in natural and engineered ecosystems both impacting climate and the efficacy of industrial process. We have chosen a suite of sample sites that together capture key underexplored niches in the methanosphere. alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

name: Freshwater sediment methanotrophic microbial communities from Lake Washington under simulated oxygen tension - Sediment Metagenome 40_LOW7

alt_names.name: Freshwater sediment methanotrophic microbial communities from Lake Washington under simulated oxygen tension
Freshwater sediment methanotrophic microbial communities from Lake Washington under simulated oxygen tension -  40_LOW7
freshwater sediment metagenome

description: In Lake Washington sediment, oxidation of methane takes place within the top 0.7-0.8 cm layer characterized by steep countergradients of methane and oxygen. The complex community of Lake Washington sediment is expected to resolve into simple communities consisting of only a few functional types, based on Oxygen tension. Methane-oxidizing communities in this part of the sediment consist of not only bona fide methanotrophs, predominantly Methylobacter species, but also species not known to be capable of methane oxidation, most notably Methylotenera. Our hypothesis is that communities and not single functional types (the methanotrophs) are involved in methane metabolism, through cooperative behavior.We further elaborated on this hypothesis by measuring the composition of microcosms incubated long-term with methane as the sole source of carbon and energy, demonstrating that methanotrophs, predominantly Methylobacter species, formed stable communities with satellite (non-methanotroph) organisms, which represented significant proportions of total communities. This proposal is specifically addressing the question of how such communities are formed and what processes take place and influence the specific composition of such communities, and what factors are involved in cooperative behavior between methanotrophs and non-methanotroph heterotrophs in these communities. The communities will be cultured in lab under two different incubation conditions, with a single variable being oxygen tension. One oxygen condition will mimic the upper part of the oxygen gradient ('high’ oxygen tension), as measured in native lake sediment, and the other will mimic the tension in the lower part of the gradient ('low’ oxygen tension).

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description: The methanome comprises genomic information distributed across organisms that either produce or consume methane as part of their metabolic repertoire. The methanome thus encodes information that regulates methane cycling in natural and engineered ecosystems both impacting climate and the efficacy of industrial process. We have chosen a suite of sample sites that together capture key underexplored niches in the methanosphere. Data arising from this study will provide an information reservoir for researchers and educators interested in exploring diversity and metabolic complexity of natural and engineered microbial communities. Information on ecology and niche adaptation of methanogens and methanotrophs will provide key information critical to incorporating microbial traits into predictive models of global methane budgets.

alt_names.name: A genome-wide sequence-indexed collection of Brachypodium distachyon mutants

description: Model systems such as Drosophila, Arabidopsis, and yeast benefit from collections of sequence-indexed genetic stocks with known mutations in practically every gene in the genome. Such collections have been elusive in grass systems such as maize and rice. To rapidly increase the utility of Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) as a model grass system, we propose to sequence three complementary mutant collections. Two collections were created using chemical mutagens (sodium azide [NaN3] or methanesulfonic acid ethyl ester [EMS]) that both induce many single base substitutions. The third collection was created by high-energy particle bombardment with fast neutron (FN) radiation.

alt_names.name: Bacterial and archaeal communities from various locations to study Microbial Dark Matter (Phase II)

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.

description: The objective of this project is to characterize the microbial communities in restored wetlands and evaluate their impact on long-term carbon sequestration. Restoration of wetlands has the potential to remove significant amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, due to rapid accumulation of emergent vegetation and low rates of biomass decomposition in the anoxic soil. Most of the long-term carbon storage takes place in the soil or sediment, yet little is known about the belowground microbial communities that are likely key determinants of the relative balance between carbon storage and atmospheric recycling. Thus I propose to study the functional and phylogenetic evolution of belowground microbial communities in newly restored freshwater and marine wetlands using powerful genomics approaches enabled by next-generation DNA sequencing technologies. The objective of this project is to characterize the microbial communities in restored wetlands and evaluate their impact on long-term carbon sequestration. Restoration of wetlands has the potential to remove significant amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, due to rapid accumulation of emergent vegetation and low rates of biomass decomposition in the anoxic soil. Most of the long-term carbon storage takes place in the soil or sediment, yet little is known about the belowground microbial communities that are likely key determinants of the relative balance between carbon storage and atmospheric recycling. Thus I propose to study the functional and phylogenetic evolution of belowground microbial communities in newly restored freshwater and marine wetlands using powerful genomics approaches enabled by next-generation DNA sequencing technologies. There are three major sub-projects planned for sequencing, each with their own needs. The first is a study of historic and restored wetlands along the salinity gradient of the San Francisco Bay, which will require itag sequencing of up to 184 samples and metagenome and metatranscriptome sequencing of 92 samples. The second is a study of the impact of different carbon and nitrogen levels on microbial communities and carbon cycling in a rice field, which will require itag and metagenome sequencing of up to 92 samples. The third is a study of the changes that occur in microbial communities over the course of a wetland restoration, which will require itag sequencing of up to 368 samples and metagenome and metatranscriptome sequencing of up to 92 samples. Restoration of wetlands has many benefits besides carbon sequestration, including reversing land subsidence on islands drained for agriculture, providing wildlife habitat and improving water quality. As a result dozens of projects to restore degraded or drained wetlands are underway or planned in the San Francisco Bay-Delta region alone. One such project, carried out by the USGS on deeply subsided Twitchell Island in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, has demonstrated a carbon sequestration rate of 1 kg per meter squared per year, which is comparable to if not greater than that achieved through tropical reforestation. Salt marshes have been suggested to have even greater carbon sequestering potential due to their very low methane production.

description: Reconstructing bacterial and archaeal genomes has revolutionized our understanding of microbial metabolism as well as evolutionary processes, and significantly sped up discoveries made in bioprospecting. The vast majority of bacterial and archaeal genomes sequenced to date are of rather limited phylogenetic diversity as they were largely chosen as based on their physiology and/ or medical importance. These findings gave rise to the initiation of the Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea (GEBA) Project (Wu et al 2009), which populated the tree of life with phylogenetically diverse reference genomes.Following into the footsteps of the GEBA project, we initiated the Microbial Dark Matter (MDM) Project in 2011 to massively expand genomic representation further by targeting 200 representatives of candidate phyla (phyla proposed on the basis of environmental sequences that have no, or very few cultivated representatives) via high throughout single-cell sequencing. The insight derived from the ~200 MDM genomes belonging to 28 major uncharted branches of the tree were invaluable (Rinke at al 2013), providing a first glimpse into the coding potential and the phylogeny of candidate phyla. The single-cell data enabled us to resolve numerous intra- and inter-phylum level relationships and propose new superphyla. In addition we proposed names for 18 candidate phyla for which we greatly expanded sequence space.  Here we propose phase II of the MDM project to further deepen our understanding of dark matter by targeting 1000 genomes from candidate phyla. Habitats of highest phylogenetic diversity (PD) value, as based on SSU rRNA surveys, are selected for single-cell sorting and shotgun metagenomics.  Thousands to tens of thousands of single cells will be anonymously sorted, whole genomes will be amplified and screened by SSU rRNA PCR and sequencing to allow their taxonomic placement and selection for the draft genome sequencing. We propose to only target taxonomic groups within candidate phyla with no or few sequenced representatives to maximize phylogenetic coverage, the selection of which will in part be driven by the outcome of the single-cell sorts.We moreover propose to generate metagenome shotgun data for each sampling site undergoing single-cell sorting.  Single cell genomes will be assembled and QC?d by single-cell specific pipelines previously developed at the JGI. Genomes will be assembled from metagenomes by algorithms developed in the Hugenholtz laboratory. The resulting genome sequences of candidate phyla representatives generated in this project will then be used for metabolic reconstruction to assess functional diversity and link these to the habitat metadata. Genomes will be mined for unique and unexpected functions. Population genomes will be used for pangenome analysis of natural populations to assess heterogeneity and deepen our insights into population structure. Lastly, including our genomes as part of the reference database, we aim to carry out large-scale phylogenetic anchoring analysis of all public metagenomes to study co-occurrence patterns in shotgun sequenced habitats worldwide.   Based on phylogenetic diversity analysis of existing SSU rRNA data, ecosystem DOE-relevance and sample access and availability, we selected a target list of 12 environments. All samples harbour a high percentage of candidate phyla. Two of these environments (Sakinaw Lake and Etoliko lagoon) were part of our previous work and SAGs for sequencing as well as metagenomic sequence data are already in hand. For the additional target environments, various Co-PIs will be responsible for providing sample for both, single-cell sequencing (cryo-preserved frozen stocks) and metgenome sequencing (extracted DNA) according to Bigelow and JGI instructions. Samples will be processed at the DOE JGI and with the assistance of the Woyke lab.
